newsitem.title: USA: Swiss shared in looted Nazi gold from Italy-memo.
newsitem.headline: Swiss shared in looted Nazi gold from Italy-memo.

text.p: Swiss banks, with the consent of Swiss authorities, had the Nazis deliver $12 million worth of looted Italian government gold to them in 1944 to pay off a war-time loan, according to a previously secret State Department document released on Monday.

The 30-page 1946 memo is the first document found in more than a year-long search of the National Archives in which U.S. diplomats directly accused the Swiss of actively encouraging the Germans to take gold for them, World Jewish Congress (WJC) investigators said in releasing the document.

WJC Vice President Kalman Sultanik, whose organisation has been combing the archives to trace the accounts of Holocaust victims, said: "This is breathtaking. If these accusations are true, this was not a commercial bank transaction but a Mafia-like transaction."

Previous documents, which have created a public relations nightmare for Switzerland, have painted a portrait of Swiss banks acting as Hitler's money-launderers -- accepting looted gold from the Germans in return for Swiss francs that the Nazis used to buy war materials and other goods to extend the war.

The latest document said that in January 1944, as the Allies were taking over most of Italy but the Fascists and Nazis were holding on to the north of the country, the Swiss National Bank became worried about whether a credit of 150 million Swiss Francs (about $33 million) a consortium of Swiss banks made to the Mussolini government would be paid off.
Two-thirds of that loan was secured by Italian government paper and one-third by gold.

The bank's president solicited the aid of Reichsbank Vice President Emil Puhl "in arranging for the transportation of a certain part of the Italian gold stocks to Switzerland," the document said in a section headlined, "Swiss Participation of the Looting of Italian Gold."

It said the Swiss pressed the Germans to ship the entire amount of gold that had been pledged as collateral, an estimated $12.1 million, and the transfer took place only after "Azzolini, the Fascist governor of the Banca d'Italia of the so-called Italian Republican government set up by Mussolini, had given his consent."

The document said that, according to Puhl, the entire banking and financial system of northern Italy was at that time under Nazi control and no gold transfer could be accomplished without German assistance or authorisation.
"It was the German government and the Reichsbank which provided for the transport of the gold to the Swiss border," the document said.

It said Puhl, who was tried after the war at the Nuremberg War Crimes tribunal, said the German decision to help the Swiss "represented a considerable concession to Switzerland on the part of the Germans, who were at the time taking over the Italian gold reserves for their own purposes."

Germany agreed to help the Swiss only because it wanted the Swiss government to continue its banking relationship, it said. The Swiss National Bank, "with the clearance of Swiss authorities," acted for a consortium of Swiss banks including Credit Suisse, the Union Bank of Switzerland, the Basler Handelsbank and the Eidgenossische Bank, it said.
There was an international uproar last month when it was discovered that records of the Eidgenossische Bank had been shredded in violation of Swiss law.

The 30-page document, a briefing paper for U.S. negotiators trying to get looted gold returned from Switzerland, also details how the Swiss accepted millions of dollars worth of gold taken by the Nazis from Belgium, Luxembourg, Yugoslavia and former Czechoslovakia.

In the Czechoslovak case, the document alleged that shortly after Hitler annexed Sudetenland, German Reichsbank officals had the Swiss National Bank simply transfer to its account gold from the Czechoslovak account that it had on deposit. It could have refused because Czechoslovakia was still an independent country at the time.

The document said the Swiss National Bank transferred 1,013 gold bars worth $14 million from its Czechoslovak account to its German account. The Germans wanted the gold to back the conversion of currency in Sudetenland to German marks from Czechoslovak currency. The transfer was made a time when Czechoslovakia was about to collapse.
